oneSentence: The approximate point up to which a model’s training-derived background is expected to be current, while newer events and facts may be absent unless added another way.
plainExplanation:
A model is trained on large collections of text and other data. Training usually uses selected material assembled up to an approximate date or period. This is often called the knowledge cutoff, training cutoff, or cut-off date.

What goes in is selected training data: books, websites, articles, code, and other sources mostly collected before the cutoff. During training, the model’s parameters, the internal numerical settings shaped by that process, are adjusted using the data. What comes out is a model that can generate useful text, but whose training-derived factual background may be outdated.

This does not mean the model cannot discuss later events. It may produce guesses, repeat patterns, or use information supplied in the prompt. But without a dependable external source, later claims should not be treated as reliable.

A context window is the input and prior output the model can use at one time. Retrieval-augmented generation can supply relevant passages at use time, including newer material. A model version is a named release whose documentation may state a cutoff. The cutoff itself concerns approximate temporal coverage of training.

everydayAnalogy.title: A school atlas printed last year
everydayAnalogy.story: A teacher in Nairobi gives students a printed world atlas published in 2024. In class, a student asks about a railway line opened in 2025. The atlas can still help with country names, borders shown at publication, and older transport routes, but it will not include the new line unless the teacher also brings a newer handout. If a student guesses the answer from older maps, the guess might sound sensible and still be wrong.

mapping.analogyElement: student guess based on older maps
mapping.aiElement: model output that sounds plausible without being up to date

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A printed atlas is fixed and visible, while a model stores patterns in numerical parameters rather than pages you can inspect directly. Also, an atlas does not generate new sentences, but a model does, so it can produce fluent guesses about post-cutoff events even when it has no dependable built-in record of them.

visual.title: What a knowledge cutoff does and does not mean
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, the reader should be able to explain that the cutoff limits built-in training knowledge, not the amount of text a model can read now, and not whether current documents can be added separately.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes: older data collected before a marked date, training, the model, and a user question about a later event. A side branch shows optional current documents added at use time. Read top row left to right, then compare the answer path without retrieval and with retrieval.

steps.label: 1. Data before the date
steps.explanation: Show a calendar marker such as 'cutoff: June 2024'. Only source material from before that point goes into training.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a stack of documents on the left with small date tags before the cutoff line; place a bold vertical date marker beside them.

steps.label: 2. Training shapes the model
steps.explanation: The model’s parameters are adjusted using those earlier sources. This forms its built-in background patterns.
steps.visualInstruction: Connect the document stack to a centre box labelled 'training', then to a box labelled 'model parameters'.

steps.label: 3. Ask about something newer
steps.explanation: A user asks about an event after the cutoff, such as 'What changed in 2025?' The built-in knowledge may be incomplete or outdated.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a question bubble to the right with a date after the cutoff; connect it to the model box.

steps.label: 4. Two answer paths
steps.explanation: Without added current sources, the reply may be uncertain or wrong. With approved current documents retrieved at use time, the answer can be grounded in newer material.
steps.visualInstruction: Split into two arrows: top arrow directly to an answer box marked 'may be outdated'; lower arrow passes through a box labelled 'current documents retrieved now' to an answer box marked 'uses newer sources'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each box to reveal a short note: 'training-time knowledge', 'user-time question', 'not the same as context window', and 'retrieval can add newer information'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-stage flow. First, documents dated before a clear cutoff line are collected. Second, those documents are used in training, which shapes the model’s parameters. Third, a user asks about an event dated after the cutoff. Fourth, the diagram splits into two paths: if no current documents are added, the answer may rely on older training patterns and may be outdated; if current documents are retrieved at use time, the answer can use newer information. The diagram also signals that this is different from the context window, which is not shown as a date limit.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static left-to-right flow with the same four stages and the two final branches visible at once, using labels and colour contrast instead of animation.

workedExample.scenario: A desk officer at Headquarters asks an approved assistant to summarise changes in a revised draft circulated last week, for talking points needed before an afternoon first reading.
workedExample.input: User prompt: “Summarise the main changes in the revised draft circulated last week.” No draft or link is provided.
process: The model’s stated knowledge cutoff predates circulation of the revised draft.
The prompt does not contain the draft, and the assistant has no retrieval connection to the document system.
The model may rely on an earlier version, infer plausible changes or invent details that sound consistent with previous text.
The officer supplies the authoritative circulated draft through an approved method and asks the assistant to compare it with the earlier version, with references to the relevant paragraphs.
workedExample.result: The cutoff explains why the model cannot reliably know the revised text from its training background. Once the current draft is supplied at inference time, the assistant can work from that text, subject to access controls and human verification.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: During a lessons-learned exercise after an assistant pilot, an ombudsman case officer at a shared services centre reviews a draft note for the file before close of business. The draft describes an intake workflow that was replaced after the model’s knowledge cutoff.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The newer workflow did not enter the model’s training-derived parameters merely because it was circulated internally. The officer must provide the current instruction through an approved source or correct the draft directly. A longer prompt alone does not make the model’s background more current.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not put names, contact details, allegations, case narratives or attachments into a tool that is not explicitly approved for ombudsman case material. For an approved tool, use de-identified extracts and the minimum necessary content under the office’s confidentiality requirements.

whyItMatters: The cutoff affects whether an answer may be outdated. That matters when you judge risk, choose whether to trust a draft, and decide when you need current documents or human checking. It also helps you ask better questions of vendors: what date does built-in knowledge reach, and what approved method adds newer information? Without that clarity, people may assume a fluent answer is current when it is not.
whereYouMayHearIt: A vendor demo during an AI procurement meeting
A lessons-learned session after an assistant pilot
An ICT governance board review of a model card
A staff briefing before an approved assistant is rolled out

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the cutoff is old, the model cannot say anything about newer events.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It can still generate text about newer events by guessing from older patterns or by using information supplied in the prompt or retrieved from another source. The issue is reliability, not silence.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Knowledge cutoff means the system stops reading after a certain date in the conversation.
commonMisconceptions.correction: That confuses cutoff with context window. The context window is the amount of text the system can process in one exchange. Knowledge cutoff is the latest date of the data used during training.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model mentions a cutoff date, every fact before that date is accurate.
commonMisconceptions.correction: No. Training data can contain errors, gaps, bias, or conflicting information. A cutoff only tells you the latest likely training period, not the quality of everything before it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Connecting a model to the internet removes the cutoff.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It can reduce the problem for some questions by adding newer sources at use time, but the model’s built-in training background still comes from an earlier period. The quality then depends on the retrieved sources and system design.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is the approximate date up to which the model’s training-derived background may be current. Newer facts may be missing unless added another way.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: During pretraining, a model is optimised on a corpus assembled up to an approximate time boundary. That boundary is commonly described as the knowledge cutoff. Information after that date is generally not represented in the model’s training-derived parameters. Newer information can be incorporated through additional training or fine-tuning, or supplied at inference time through retrieval or user-provided context. The term refers to temporal coverage of training data, not context capacity, conversation history, or automatic access to live external sources. Because models generate outputs from learned statistical patterns rather than a dated fact table, post-cutoff answers may still appear confident even when unsupported by current evidence.

keyTakeaway: A knowledge cutoff marks the approximate recency of the model’s training-derived background. It does not limit prompt length or prevent the model from using current information supplied through approved retrieval or context.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes a knowledge cutoff?
options: The latest date of information likely included in the model’s training data
The maximum number of words the model can read in one prompt
The date when the model account was created
A guarantee that all earlier facts are correct
quickCheck.explanation: A knowledge cutoff is about the time range of training data. It is not the context window, not an account setting, and not a guarantee of accuracy. Even before the cutoff, errors can remain; after the cutoff, newer facts may need retrieval or human checking.

issues.problem: This presents the cutoff as a precise latest point covered by the training data. In practice, the stated cutoff is an approximate boundary for expected training-derived coverage. Sources can have uneven dates, older gaps, and references to later periods.
issues.fix: The approximate point up to which a model’s training-derived background is expected to be current, while newer events and facts may be absent unless added another way.

issues.problem: The explanation repeatedly treats the cutoff as an exact boundary. It also defines the context window as text handled in "one exchange", which excludes relevant prior input and output, and says retrieval-augmented generation adds current documents even though retrieved passages are not necessarily current. It also claims to distinguish related terms but does not distinguish a knowledge cutoff from a model version.

issues.problem: The claim that an atlas published in 2024 "will not include" a railway opened in 2025 is too absolute. The atlas could show a planned or incomplete railway before it opens.
issues.fix: Replace "but it will not include the new line" with "but it may not show the new line as open".

issues.problem: The visual teaches a hard date boundary by saying only material from before the marker enters training. That is stronger than a knowledge cutoff supports and hides uneven source coverage.
issues.fix: In step 1, use: "Show an illustrative marker such as 'cutoff: June 2024'. Training coverage is approximate and may vary by source." In the accessibility description, replace the first sentence with: "First, documents largely dated before an approximate cutoff are collected."

issues.problem: The correction again defines a context window as what the system processes in "one exchange". The supplied definition includes input and prior output available while producing the next response, which may span multiple turns.
issues.fix: That confuses cutoff with context window. The context window is the input and prior output the system can use at one time while generating a response. Knowledge cutoff concerns the approximate time coverage of training data.

issues.problem: This again describes the cutoff as an exact date up to which the background was learned rather than an approximate indicator of expected temporal coverage.
issues.fix: It is the approximate date up to which the model’s training-derived background may be current. Newer facts may be missing unless added another way.
